objective: recognise angles as a description of a turn.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show the students the Explore task and talk about how the pieces of the shelter meet. Show students that angles are created by two straight lines turning from the same point by opening and closing two rulers that stay connected at a point. It is important that students understand that an angle is the amount of rotation (turn) to move one side of the angle to the other side about its vertex. Ask the students when to tell you when to stop opening the rulers to create angles similar to those in the shelter. Guide them to see that an angle is formed when two straight lines meet at a point and we can mark that to show it clearly.
Explain to students that we can differentiate angles by labelling them. Show the students the first image in Master. Ask them to label the angles a, b and c. What can they say about the amount of turn each of the angles show?
During Guided Practice, students are making angles using rulers. Ask them which rulers make angles and why. How do they know? Students are also asked to make angles that are bigger and smaller than the one shown. What does this mean? Tell them your friend said all you have to do is make longer lines. Is this correct? Does the length of the line have anything to do with the angle they make? Allow students to explore this idea.
formative_assessment:
identify angles as two lines that meet at a point.
Students can identify an angle by labelling it with a letter.
Students can use concrete materials to make angles.
Students can draw angles using a ruler.
content_priority:
This lesson can be combined with Lesson 2.
We suggest completing Lesson 3 before Lessons 1 and 2.

objective: recognise angles as a property of shape.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with a variety of 2D shapes. Show them the Explore task and ask them how many angles they can see for each shape. Let them discuss this. Then tell them your friend said that knowing the number of sides a shape is helpful in finding the number of angles. Is this true? Work through Master and ask them if they can see a pattern that applies to all shapes. Ask them to construct a chart and record the number of sides and angles that each shape has. Can they see a pattern? What is it?
Tell students that when two straight sides of a shape meet at a point they form an angle. The point or corner at which they meet is called a vertex. Students should be encouraged to use these terms when describing shapes in this chapter.
Students have been introduced to the names of some 2D shapes in Year 2. However, they may not have learned the name pentagon for a 5-sided shape.
During Guided Practice, students are identifying the number of sides and angles of different shapes, and then marking the angles in each shape.
formative_assessment:
identify angles as two lines that meet at a point.
Students can identify an angle by labelling it with a letter.
Students can mark an angle.
Students can relate the number of sides of a shape to the number of angles in that shape.
content_priority:
This is a key lesson.
We suggest completing this lesson before Lessons 1 and 2 and taking students outdoors to find angles in shapes.
This lesson can be combined with Lesson 4.

approach:

During Guided Practice, students are identifying right angles using their checker.

objective: identify an acute angle as a smaller angle than a right angle.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with their right-angle checkers (rulers). Show them the Explore task and allow them to inspect the gate shown to determine whether or not it has any right angles. Ask them to mark the right angles on the gate. Then ask them if they can identify angles that are smaller than a right angle. Show them how they can use their right-angle checker to do this and ask them to mark these angles. Tell them these angles are called 'acute' angles.
Guide students to see that right angles are all the same size, whereas acute angles come in different sizes.
During Guided Practice, students are drawing a right angle, an acute angle, identifying right angles and then finding right angles and acute angles in shapes.
formative_assessment:
name right angles correctly when they see one.
Students can mark right angles.
Students can use a right-angle tester to identify right angles.
Students can name acute angles correctly when they see one.
Students can mark acute angles.
Students can use a right-angle checker to identify acute angles.

objective: identify an obtuse angle as a greater angle than a right angle.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Ask them to find all the angles they can see in the clock faces, paying special attention to the question that asks them to find the clock with hands showing an angle larger than a right angle. Structure the learning as in the Master section, so that students are identifying the right angles and the acute angles before looking at 5 o'clock. 5 o'clock has a special angle that looks bigger than a right angle. Allow students to talk about this angle and see if they know what it is called and what makes it special.
Explain that a smaller or larger angle is made by making a smaller or larger rotation (turn) to move one side of the angle to the other side about its vertex. Compare angles by identifying whether the turn is less than or greater than the other.
Obtuse angles are larger than 90°. What must that mean about a right angle and an acute angle? Is one of them equal to 90°? Is one of them smaller? What would make the most sense? Allow students some time to discuss this.
During Guided Practice, students are drawing the angles they have learnt, and then identifying whether angles are larger or smaller than a right angle. They will be naming all the angles they have learnt, followed by finding angles in a shape and explaining their answers.

objective: identify right angles and recognise that two right angles make a half-turn, three angles make three-quarters of a turn and four angles make a complete turn.
approach:
To begin this lesson, enlarge the Explore task and display it in front of the class. Ask students to use right-angle turns to move the animal around the game board. Tell them that to get started, your friend said they need to make a right-angle turn clockwise. What would this do to the animal? Allow them to continue playing the game using right-angle turns.
After some time, tell them your friend played the game differently and introduce the terms 'half turn' and 'quarter turn'. What do they mean? How would you do a half turn? Is it like any of the turns you have done using right angles? Allow them to discuss how 1, 2 and 3 right-angle turns might look like when completed, using fractions to describe the movements (e.g. quarter, half and three-quarters).
During Guided Practice, students are describing the turns of triangles using right-angle turns and fractions.
formative_assessment:
use the term 'right angle' to describe a turn.
Students can use the terms 'clockwise' and 'anticlockwise' to describe a turn.
Students can use fractions to describe a turn (e.g. quarter, half and three-quarters).
Students can determine where the starting point is before giving instructions.
national_curriculum:
Turn, and describe how far an object or person has turned, using full, half, quarter, and three-quarter turns as benchmarks.
Recognise that angles can be measured in degrees, using 90, 180, and 360 degrees as benchmarks.

objective: use knowledge of angles to solve problems.
approach:
Mind Workout
Students finish drawing a seven-sided shape based on known information about the number of different angles it has.
Maths Journal
Students draw the shape shown and mark the different angles. Students should explain how they found each one.
Review
Complete this with students as a chapter summary, and determine if any of them need extra support.
